newsitem.title: UK: Mark steadies in Europe before French elections.
newsitem.headline: Mark steadies in Europe before French elections.

text.p: The mark steadied against other European currencies, holding the bulk of gains it made this week before the French elections Sunday.
The mark was supported just shy of 3.38 French francs amid expectations the opposition Socialist party will wrest power from the ruling centre-right coalition.

Still, traders don't expect the mark to rise too much further given both the French elections and a row between the Bundesbank and the German government have cast a shadow over the outlook for European economic and monetary union.
"The market has got itself positioned for the French elections and it seems to prefer to be long of marks," said Brian Martin, the chief currency strategist at BZW.
Mark/Paris was last at 3.3793/98 from 3.3804/09 late Thursday in Europe. Mark/lira was quoted at 992.50/3.00 from 991.90/2.20 late Thursday.
The Bundesbank and the German government clashed over Bonn's plan to revalue the central bank's assets in a bid to ensure Germany qualifies for EMU.
The dispute temporarily undermined the mark earlier this week amid speculation it made Germany more vulnerable to being railroaded into a broad EMU.
Speculation that Germany may prefer to postpone the launch of the European single currency than give in to French demands for a broad EMU kept the mark buoyed, however.

Nick Parsons, the currency strategist at Paribas Capital Markets, said speculation the Bundesbank will raise interest rates sooner than expected to reassert its independence could also emerge as a support for the mark in the coming weeks.
"Any perception of threat to their credibility could lead to higher rates, for which the government could be blamed," he said.

Rumours Italy's credit rating was about to be downgraded propelled the mark to a one-month high of 995.25 lire Friday. The German currency pared gains after the rumour was denied by credit agencies, and then extended its losses after the Italian cabinet approved a three-year economic plan which aims to ensure Italy is a founding member of EMU.

Italian prime minister Romano Prodi said Italy is aiming to reduce its deficit to 2.8 percent of its gross domestic product in 1998, below the 3 percent required of EMU entrants. -Swaha Pattanaik, London Forex Desk +44 171 542 6284
